intro.title: Preserving Memory Through Data
intro.paragraph1: This project builds upon Dr. Christoph Kreutzmüller's groundbreaking research documented in 'Final Sale: The Destruction of Jewish Commercial Activity in Nazi Germany' (2015). His decade-long work with the Leo Baeck Institute created an unprecedented archive of Jewish businesses across Germany.
intro.paragraph2: Our interactive map transforms this scholarly database into an accessible digital experience, documenting Jewish-owned businesses in Berlin from 1900 to 1945. Each marker represents a family enterprise - from corner shops to department stores - that formed the economic fabric of the city.
intro.paragraph3: Navigate through time to explore how these businesses thrived, struggled, and ultimately faced forced closure. By combining historical research with modern visualization, we aim to make this important history accessible to new generations.

kreutzmuller.title: Dr. Christoph Kreutzmüller's Pioneering Work
kreutzmuller.description: This project builds directly upon Dr. Kreutzmüller's groundbreaking 2015 study 'Final Sale: The Destruction of Jewish Commercial Activity in Nazi Germany.' His team spent over a decade meticulously documenting the systematic destruction of Jewish businesses across Germany.
kreutzmuller.methodology: Working with the Leo Baeck Institute, Dr. Kreutzmüller and his researchers analyzed thousands of archival documents, municipal records, trade directories, and survivor testimonies to create an unprecedented database of Jewish commercial life before and during the Nazi period.

database.title: The Leo Baeck Institute Database
database.description: The comprehensive database housed at the Leo Baeck Institute contains detailed records of thousands of Jewish businesses, including registration documents, 'Aryanization' records, forced sales documentation, and personal testimonies from business owners and their families.
database.scope: This invaluable scholarly resource documents not just the businesses themselves, but the human stories behind them - families displaced, livelihoods destroyed, and communities forever changed.

transformation.title: From Archive to Accessibility
transformation.description: StoryTimeMaps transforms this scholarly database into an interactive digital experience, making Dr. Kreutzmüller's research accessible to students, educators, and the general public while maintaining historical accuracy and academic rigor.

hero.title: A Museum Exhibit for Berlin's Lost Businesses
hero.subtitle: From a digital archive of 10,021 enterprises to a public space of memory
hero.visionDescription: We envision a museum exhibit that brings the documented history of Berlin's Jewish businesses out of the database and into a shared physical space — where visitors stand before a living map of the city, follow a single family enterprise through the years, and witness how a vibrant commercial world was systematically dismantled between 1900 and 1945.
hero.ctaDescription: We are seeking museum, cultural, and educational partners — and the funding — to turn this vision into a permanent and travelling exhibit.

experience.title: What Visitors Experience
experience.subtitle: An interactive journey through a vanished commercial world
experience.card1Description: A large touch-screen map of Berlin where every marker is a real documented business. Visitors explore neighbourhoods, zoom into streets, and surface the stories beneath their feet.
experience.card2Description: A timeline from 1900 to 1945 lets visitors watch businesses open, thrive, decline, and face forced closure — making the scale and pace of persecution visible at a glance.
experience.card3Description: Behind each marker is a family enterprise — a tailor, a bookseller, a department store. Detailed stories restore names, faces, and livelihoods to the historical record.
experience.card4Description: Built multilingual from the start (English, German, and Yiddish), the exhibit welcomes Berliners, descendants, students, and international visitors alike.

concept.title: One map. Three dimensions.
concept.intro: The archive behind this site is a list of names, addresses and dates. The map turns that list back into a city — one you can stand in, move through, and watch change.
concept.placeTitle: Every dot is a real address
concept.placeText: Each business is mapped to the street where it actually stood — tailors in Mitte, publishers in Kreuzberg, department stores on Kurfürstendamm. Zoom in and the dots become shops with names, owners and stories.
concept.timeTitle: Drag the years, watch the city change
concept.timeText: A time slider runs beneath the map from 1900 to 1945. Slide it and businesses open, struggle and vanish around you — the boycott of 1933, the forced transfers of 1938, the end of the war.
concept.fateText: At any moment, each dot shows the state of that business: operating normally, under growing pressure in its final years, or closed — liquidated, seized, or destroyed.

memorial.quote: Behind every dot: a family, a livelihood, a place where Berlin bought its bread, its books, its winter coats. This map exists so that they are not reduced to a number.

history.note: This was not a collapse but a campaign: boycott, legal exclusion, forced sale, destruction. Each step is visible on the map as a wave of color moving through the city.

data.intro: Every figure below comes from the same archive the map draws from. The shape of the chart is the history: pressure building through the 1930s, then the catastrophe of 1938.

about.title: A digital memorial with a physical future
about.mission: StoryTimeMaps set out to map the formerly Jewish-owned businesses of Berlin from verified historical records and archival imagery — and then to carry that memory back into the physical city: through memorial plaques at the original addresses, and a public museum exhibit.
about.sourceText: Every record comes from the Datenbank jüdischer Gewerbebetriebe in Berlin at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin — the scholarly database grounded in Dr. Christoph Kreutzmüller’s research — with archival material informed by the Leo Baeck Institute.
about.fact1: All 10,021 records re-verified against the original source in 2026
about.fact2: Every record carries its source link and a verification date
about.fact3: Roughly nine in ten businesses plotted at their exact street address
about.fact4: Multilingual from the ground up: English, German and Yiddish
about.phaseMapText: The interactive memorial you are looking at: every documented business, searchable and explorable in three languages.
about.phasePlaquesText: Fifteen plaques are fully designed — each carrying a QR code that links the street back to the business’s story. Outreach to building owners is underway.
about.phaseTourText: Fifteen addresses in a modelled 1930s Berlin. Scroll, and the camera flies from one storefront to the next as the years advance from 1925 to 1945.
about.phaseExhibitText: A touch-screen exhibit version of the map is built and running, designed for kiosk display. We are seeking museum and cultural partners to host it.
about.phaseBeyondText: A Frankfurt pilot of 57 businesses shows the model extends to other German cities.
